client: Lately, I’ve been feeling really overwhelmed at my new marketing job. The deadlines are so tight, and I keep comparing myself to my colleagues who seem to know exactly what they’re doing. I’m not sure therapy can really help with this—it feels like the problem is just that I’m not good enough for the role.
therapist: It sounds like you’re carrying a lot of pressure and self-doubt, especially when comparing yourself to others—that must feel exhausting. Let’s explore what’s behind that thought of “not being good enough”—what evidence do you have for and against it?

client: I guess the evidence against it is that I did get hired, so someone thought I was capable. But the evidence for it is that I’m constantly second-guessing myself and making mistakes. It’s hard to focus on the positive when I feel like I’m barely keeping up. I don’t know if just listing evidence will actually change how I feel, though—it feels like the problem is deeper than that.
therapist: It’s understandable to feel that way when the weight of self-doubt feels so heavy—acknowledging both sides of the evidence is a great first step, though. Let’s dig deeper into what “barely keeping up” means to you—what would a manageable pace look like, and how might that differ from your current expectations?

client: A manageable pace would probably mean not feeling like I’m drowning every day, but I don’t even know how to get there. My expectations are just to meet deadlines and not mess up, but that feels impossible already. I guess I’m worried that if I slow down or lower my expectations, I’ll fall even further behind or look incompetent to my team.
therapist: It sounds like you’re caught between the fear of falling behind and the exhaustion of trying to keep up—that’s a really tough place to be. Let’s explore what “looking competent” means to you—do you think others on your team might also feel this pressure, or could they have moments of uncertainty too?

client: I guess I haven’t really thought about whether others feel this way too—it’s hard to imagine because they all seem so confident. But I suppose everyone has moments of uncertainty, right? Still, it’s hard to shake the feeling that I’m the only one struggling. Even if others feel pressure, it doesn’t really change how overwhelmed I feel right now.
therapist: It’s easy to assume others are more confident when we’re only seeing the surface, but you’re right—everyone has moments of uncertainty, even if they don’t show it. Let’s focus on what might help *you* feel less overwhelmed—what’s one small step you could take today to ease the pressure, even just a little?

client: I guess one small step could be to take a short break during the day to clear my head, but it feels like I don’t even have time for that. I’m always rushing from one task to the next, and I feel guilty if I’m not constantly working. Plus, I’m not sure a break would really make a difference—the workload won’t magically disappear, right?
therapist: It sounds like you’re caught in a cycle of feeling guilty for taking breaks while also feeling overwhelmed—that’s a really common struggle when work feels relentless. Let’s challenge the idea that breaks don’t make a difference—what might happen if you tried a short break and noticed how it affects your focus or mood, even just a little?

client: I guess if I took a short break, I might feel a little less tense, but I’m not sure it would help with the bigger picture. The workload is still there, and I’d probably just feel guilty for not using that time to get ahead. It’s hard to believe a few minutes would make a difference when I’m so far behind already.
therapist: It’s understandable to feel that way when the workload feels so overwhelming—guilt can make it hard to prioritize even small moments of self-care. Let’s explore how taking a short break might shift your perspective—what would it mean for you to approach this as an experiment, rather than expecting it to solve everything right away?

client: I guess approaching it as an experiment could make it feel less pressured, but I still worry it won’t change much. What if I take the break and still feel just as overwhelmed afterward? It’s hard to imagine something so small having any real impact when the workload feels so huge. I don’t know if I’d even notice a difference.
therapist: It makes sense to feel skeptical when the workload feels so big and the break so small—it’s hard to imagine how a few minutes could make a dent. Let’s treat this as a chance to gather information—what if you took a break and simply observed how it feels, without expecting it to solve everything? What might you notice about your energy or mindset, even if it’s subtle?

client: I guess I could try it and just observe, but part of me still feels like it’s a waste of time. What if I don’t notice anything different? It’s hard to believe something so small could help when I’m drowning in tasks. I don’t want to feel like I’m just avoiding the work, even for a few minutes.
therapist: It sounds like there’s a lot of guilt tied to the idea of taking a break, as if it’s avoiding the work rather than supporting you—that’s a tough mindset to shift when you’re feeling so overwhelmed. Let’s explore this as a small experiment—what if, for just a few minutes, you approached the break as a way to recharge, rather than seeing it as avoidance? What might you notice about your energy or focus afterward?

client: I guess if I framed it as recharging, it might feel less like avoidance, but I’m still not sure it would help. Even if I feel a bit calmer afterward, the work will still be waiting for me, and I’ll probably just end up feeling more stressed about the time I “lost.” It’s hard to see the point when the pressure feels so constant.
therapist: It’s understandable to feel that way when the pressure feels so unrelenting—breaks can feel like they’re adding to the stress rather than relieving it. Let’s think about it this way—what might happen if you approached the break as a way to work *more effectively*, rather than losing time? How might easing the tension help you tackle the tasks with a clearer mind?

client: I guess if I thought of the break as helping me work more effectively, it might feel less like wasted time. But I’m still skeptical—I’ve tried taking breaks before, and I just end up feeling more anxious about the tasks piling up. It’s hard to believe a few minutes will make a difference when I’m already so far behind.
therapist: It sounds like past experiences have made it hard to trust that breaks could be helpful, especially when the tasks feel so urgent—that’s completely valid. Let’s explore what might make this break feel different—what could you do during those few minutes that might help you feel more grounded, rather than more anxious?
